message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it changes with light, depth, water clarity, and what’s in the water.

| Factor | Typical Effect on Color |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) and reflects shorter wavelengths (blue, green). So very deep ocean looks deep‑blue or even black. |
| **Clarity / Suspended Particles** | Clear water lets more blue light through, giving a bright turquoise or sky‑blue hue. Turbid water with sediments or plankton scatters light and can look greenish, brownish, or even gray. |
| **Algae / Phytoplankton** | High concentrations of green algae give the water a green tint. Some blooms can make the sea look almost green‑yellow or even reddish if the algae contain pigments like phycoerythrin. |
| **Sun Angle & Weather** | On a sunny day, the sea can look bright blue or turquoise. Overcast skies or low sun angles can make it appear darker or more muted. |
| **Bottom Color** | In shallow coastal areas, the color of the sand or rocks underneath can tint the water—white sand gives a lighter, almost milky look; dark basalt can make it appear darker. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” it can range from deep navy to bright turquoise, greenish‑blue, or even brownish‑gray depending on those conditions.
